meru-china-russia-gas-talks-collapse:
Gas pricing negotiations between Russia and China over the second Power of Siberia (POS2) pipeline have collapsed.
China reportedly offered $50 per 1,000 cubic meters; Russia asked for $250, according to Korean market commentator Meru.

The numbers check out. Asia Times and bne IntelliNews both independently confirm China's $50 offer and Russia's $250 ask.
Russia's own delivery cost from its Yamal fields to China runs around $125 per 1,000 cubic meters.
China currently pays $240-280 through the existing Power of Siberia 1 line. Gazprom charges other
international buyers an average of around $420, and China's LNG import price runs around $370.
Against those numbers, China's $50 doesn't even cover Russia's delivery cost, while Russia's $250 ask
looks like a reasonable middle ground.

@@REF@@Power of Siberia 2 deadlock belies Russia-China 'no-limits' pact (Asia Times, 2026-07-16)|https://asiatimes.com/2026/07/power-of-siberia-2-deadlock-cracks-russia-china-no-limits-pact/|https://asiatimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Xi_Putin.jpg

## Meru points to a bridge dispute as the reason
Meru links the breakdown to an entirely different dispute: a rail bridge over the Tumen River, on the
China-North Korea border. Completed in April 2026, the bridge could give China access to the Sea of
Japan, but Russia's side has been slow finishing approach roads and customs facilities, and North Korea
reportedly suspects Russia is deliberately dragging its feet out of deference to China. Meru's theory
is that China's unusually low gas offer could be a signal of frustration over the bridge.

@@REF@@Tumen River bridge delay rattles North Korea (Daily NK, 2026-06-24)|https://www.dailynk.com/english/tumen-river-bridge-delay-north-korea-russia/|https://www.dailynk.com/english/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/06/tumen-river-north-korea-russia-china-border-fangchuan.jpg

The bridge dispute itself is real and independently reported. But no wire service or outlet, including
this one, connects the bridge to the gas talks. Meru himself is careful to add that China's real motive
can't be confirmed from outside.

@@CMP@@Meru's read|China's unusually low offer could be a signal of frustration or retaliation over the delayed bridge.|What other sources suggest|POS2 is still pre-construction and China is Russia's only realistic large buyer, so the lowball may just be a negotiating tactic from the side that isn't in a hurry.
The split is whether the price gap is a political message, or simply a calculation from the side with nothing to lose by waiting.

## The real leverage looks like it's somewhere else
Analysis from the Carnegie Endowment shows POS2 is still stuck at a September 2025 agreement-in-principle

Over the same period, Russia's pipeline gas exports to Europe fell 44% in 2025 alone, hitting their

TurkStream. In Carnegie's own words, "China is the only buyer capable of taking the huge quantity of

jukan-goldman-china-dram-catchup:
Goldman Sachs held an expert call with a Chinese DRAM industry insider, and semiconductor analyst Jukan relayed the key takeaways. The headline point: Chinese DRAM makers' prices have already caught up to global leaders like Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron.

## How close has it actually gotten
A direct comparison by Tom's Hardware on July 26 found CXMT's 64GB DDR5-5600 RDIMM selling for 18,999 yuan on JD.com, versus 18,595 yuan for equivalent Samsung/SK hynix modules, a gap of just 2.2%. SemiAnalysis separately found CXMT's Q1 2026 average selling prices had narrowed to within 5-10% of the big three, and that the quarter's earnings improvement came mainly from pricing (up roughly 57% quarter over quarter), not volume growth.

@@REF@@Chinese CXMT DRAM doesn't look like the budget savior many were expecting (Tom's Hardware, 2026-07-26)|https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/dram/chinese-cxmt-dram-doesnt-look-like-the-budget-savior-many-were-expecting-new-modules-enter-the-market-but-prices-still-track-the-big-three|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/Y6RXNGdt5atPtqKHjD7EUW-1280-80.jpg

## The catch: this parity is mainstream-only
Per memory vendors WCCFTech spoke to at Computex in June, this price convergence is limited to entry-level and mainstream DDR5 modules running up to 8000 MT/s. CXMT has essentially no presence in premium formats like CUDIMM, CQDIMM or MRDIMM. So "Chinese DRAM matches Samsung" is true for a slice of the lineup, not the whole thing.

"Yield" is the share of chips on a wafer that come out working. SemiAnalysis estimates CXMT's cost per bit runs more than 30% above the big three, partly because its die is around 40% larger than Samsung's, meaning fewer working chips per wafer. Charging within 2% of leader prices while carrying that much higher cost points to either eating losses to defend share, or state subsidies covering the gap. No report found actually documents subsidies covering that specific price gap, though. What is documented is capex-stage support, like a Hefei state investment vehicle funding around 80% of CXMT's Phase 1 buildout.

@@REF@@China's CXMT Is Set to Challenge DRAM Incumbents (SemiAnalysis, 2026-06-23)|https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/chinas-cxmt-is-set-to-challenge-dram|https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!II9S!,w_1200,h_675,c_fill,f_jpg,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb42b8c2b-1749-4adc-b179-57c4fdda8500_1536x1024.png

## The bigger story may be industry-wide, not subsidy-driven
A larger reason prices have converged: Samsung, SK hynix and Micron have been redirecting wafer capacity toward AI-driven HBM, tightening the overall supply of conventional DRAM industry-wide. CXMT has no HBM pivot to make, so it kept its volume relatively intact. This looks less like CXMT winning on price and more like its rivals stepping out of the way.

A technology roadmap came up too. Chinese DRAM makers are expected to make further progress on 3D-stacked DRAM in 2027, and capacity expansions in Hefei, Shanghai and Beijing are slated to be fully operational by 2028.

## Is blocking lithography alone enough
Some fabs reportedly run mostly on domestically produced Chinese equipment, with one exception: high-end lithography, the machines that etch circuit patterns onto wafers. But that chokepoint isn't just EUV. Tom's Hardware reports China began delivering domestically made immersion DUV (ArFi) tools to SMIC, Hua Hong and CXMT in 2026, though commercial-scale self-sufficiency isn't expected until the mid-2030s. ASML still holds 98.7% of the immersion DUV market.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is Chinese DRAM matching leader prices despite lower yields a loss-leading share defense, subsidy power, or simply a windfall from the industry's own pivot to HBM.

Once Samsung, SK hynix and Micron dial back HBM and return to conventional DRAM, CXMT's pricing power gets tested for real. If the gap stays around 2%, China's catch-up is real. If it widens again, this "price parity" will have been a temporary window opened by the industry's own capacity shift.
jukan-huawei-ai-chip-shipments-double:
Huawei is on track to ship around 1.5 million of its own AI accelerator chips this year, roughly double the volume it shipped in 2025, according to a Wall Street Journal report relayed by semiconductor analyst Jukan on X. The jump matters because it comes despite years of US export controls designed to cut China off from advanced chipmaking equipment and Nvidia's most powerful GPUs.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/NVIDIA_GPU.jpg/960px-NVIDIA_GPU.jpg|An AI accelerator chip. Huawei's Ascend line plugs into data center servers in a similar form factor.|Mickael Courtiade · CC BY 2.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NVIDIA_GPU.jpg

## The exact 1.5 million figure doesn't hold up under scrutiny
The original WSJ article sits behind a paywall and couldn't be verified directly. Other outlets' own shipment estimates, gathered together, tell a messier story. Bloomberg put 2025 Ascend 910C shipments at roughly 300,000 units (up to 1 million dies across the whole Ascend line) and 2026 at 600,000 units (up to 1.6 million dies). SemiAnalysis put actual 2025 shipments at 805,000 units (653,000 of them 910C). JPMorgan, cited by Tom's Hardware, put SMIC-based output at 600,000-650,000 in 2025 and 800,000-850,000 in 2026. The US Commerce Department separately estimated Huawei's 2025 capacity at under 200,000 units, three to seven times lower than the industry estimates above. No single source independently confirms "exactly 1.5 million, exactly double."

@@REF@@China's chip champions ramp up production of AI accelerators at domestic fabs, but HBM and fab production capacity are towering bottlenecks (Tom's Hardware, 2025-09-10)|https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/chinas-chip-champions-ramp-up-production-of-ai-accelerators-at-domestic-fabs-but-hbm-and-fab-production-capacity-are-towering-bottlenecks|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/yhFcLNWMWBru4ox6DxUvQG-2560-80.jpg

## The real bottleneck isn't lithography, it's HBM
Huawei's AI chips sell under the Ascend brand, and export controls first imposed in 2019 and tightened since have blocked Huawei from buying the most advanced lithography tools or importing Nvidia's top chips. But SemiAnalysis and Tom's Hardware independently point to a different constraint as the real one: high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Huawei's pre-restriction HBM stockpile, estimated at around 11.7 million stacks, was expected to run out by the end of 2025, and domestic substitute CXMT's annual capacity of roughly 2.2 million stacks supports only 250,000-400,000 910C packages. A July 2026 Bloomberg Intelligence survey still named HBM shortage as the biggest bottleneck.

@@CMP@@Common read|Export controls have starved China of AI compute, keeping it years behind.|What multiple analysts show|The real constraint on Huawei isn't lithography, it's the pre-restriction HBM stockpile running dry, and once it does, shipments could fall well short of 1.5 million.
Inside the same export-control story, analysts disagree on which specific component is actually doing the choking.

DigiTimes reported Huawei's SMIC-made 7nm-class chip yield rising from around 20% in September 2024 to around 40% in early 2025, but no updated figure beyond that could be found. That's still well below TSMC's 90%-plus yields at comparable nodes.

## Who's actually buying this volume
ByteDance reportedly planned around $5.6 billion in Ascend chip orders in December 2025, and a March 2026 Reuters report relayed by CNBC said ByteDance and Alibaba were considering orders for the newer, inference-focused Ascend 950PR. That suggests a meaningful share of what's shipping now is going to inference workloads, not frontier model training.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is Huawei's shipment jump proof that export controls failed to contain China's AI chips, or a number propped up by stockpiled memory that's about to run out.

If Huawei's HBM stockpile actually empties by the end of 2025 and shipments keep climbing anyway, that's real self-sufficiency. If shipments stall right around then, this "doubling" report will have been a one-time number borrowed from inventory that's already spent.
jukan-nand-sandisk-lta-bearish-pushback:
## What actually got sold cheap
NAND holds the photos on your phone and the files on your laptop.
It keeps them with the power off,
and Meta stacks it in data centres.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/USB_flash_drive.JPG/500px-USB_flash_drive.JPG|The USB stick in your drawer. The storage chip inside it is NAND.|Nrbelex · CC BY-SA 3.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:USB_flash_drive.JPG

NAND types differ by bits per storage cell.
TLC holds three, QLC holds four.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Cell_types_SLC-PLC_in_comparison_20211102.svg/1280px-Cell_types_SLC-PLC_in_comparison_20211102.svg.png|Bits per cell, side by side. Third from the left is TLC, fourth is QLC.|PantheraLeo1359531 · CC0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cell_types_SLC-PLC_in_comparison_20211102.svg

More bits per cell means more storage per area, so unit cost falls.
The cell also wears faster and runs slower.

QLC is the cheap end, TLC the durable one.
QLC is the one in question.

## Why sign below the going rate
A long-term agreement, or LTA, fixes volume and price years ahead.

Think of it as a phone contract.
Lock in for two years, the monthly bill drops.
The buyer promises volume, the seller shaves the price.
The fab stays busy, so both sides want it.

An LTA below the spot rate is the normal outcome, not a warning.
SanDisk plans to fill over half its shipments this way, which tilts it further.

## So is $0.38 actually cheap
SanDisk opened near $0.50 a unit, expensive for QLC and close to TLC money.

The deal settled near $0.38, a 24% cut.
@@REF@@SanDisk secures Meta NAND supply deal (Yahoo Finance, 2026-07-24)|https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/sandisk-sndk-secures-meta-nand-171417598.html|https://media.zenfs.com/en/simply_wall_st__316/4ede54afa2108a12bdee07c0b0d94a59

@@CMP@@The bear read|A 24% cut from $0.50 to $0.38. You do not discount that hard on something that sells itself.|Jukan's read|$0.50 was TLC money to begin with. $0.38 is closer to fair, and the LTA took the rest.

Same number, opposite readings, depending on where you set the baseline.

## Is the China story a demand signal
One more story props up the bear case, from China.

Module makers there were reportedly turned away selling enterprise SSDs at home.
A module maker buys NAND chips and assembles them into drives.
@@REF@@Chinese memory vendors pick homegrown YMTC and CXMT over Samsung and Micron (Tom's Hardware, 2026-06-17)|https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/ram/chinese-memory-vendors-snub-industry-giants-in-favor-of-homegrown-ram-chips-samsung-micron-and-sk-hynix-face-a-chinese-supply-chain-revolt|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/tn9gFjhWREg7FV67sMTNJY-2560-80.jpg

Jukan places the cause elsewhere.
Those clouds already buy direct from YMTC, China's own NAND maker.

No reason for a middleman differs from nothing to buy.

## Is an LTA only a safe card
Jukan treats SanDisk filling half its shipments with LTAs as a bull point.
Turn it over and it becomes a cost.

With half the volume fixed years out,
a rise in NAND prices cannot reach it.

An LTA is a floor when prices fall and a ceiling when they climb.
The more bullish on memory, the less appealing a company that pre-sold half its output.

The spread of LTAs is also hard to read as weakness.
Intel and AMD are reportedly signing CPU LTAs with Chinese customers.

Ibiden is the Japanese maker of substrates that package advanced chips.
When Samsung sought them,
Ibiden reportedly asked for LTA guarantees.

That is the buyer locking supply down.
@@REF@@Intel and AMD to sign CPU LTAs with Chinese customers (Serenity, 2026-07-23)|https://x.com/aleabitoreddit/status/2080153334888182065

## What the next two days did
Two days later the market moved the other way.

On the 27th SanDisk fell over 14% in a session,
47% below its June 22 high.
About $170 billion of market value went in a month.

None of that proves Jukan wrong on how the contract was priced.
It does say the market reads this as the cycle, not the contract.
@@REF@@SanDisk drops 14% in a day, 47% off its June high (The Kobeissi Letter, 2026-07-27)|https://x.com/KobeissiLetter/status/2081814364928057486

## What settles it
The question comes down to one thing.
Did the discount come from the contract, or from the cycle turning?
If it is the contract, this drop can reverse.
If it is the cycle, it has further to run.

Two things will tell.

If next quarter's QLC contract prints above $0.38, Jukan's read holds.
If below, $0.38 was a starting point, not a floor.

And if SanDisk's LTA share clears half,
there will be a stretch where NAND rises and this name lags.

Either way, a company with half its volume at fixed prices
rises less on the way up and sinks less on the way down.
That asymmetry comes before the direction call.
jukan-cxmt-3d-ic-niche-strategy:
The chip industry's race to boost AI performance is shifting from process shrinks to 3D stacking, which fuses logic and memory in one package, and Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are staying cautious about commercializing it while China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) moves to claim the niche, semiconductor analyst Jukan reports.

## What actually separates 3D IC from HBM
HBM stacks DRAM on a base logic die that mostly handles input/output and signal routing, then connects to a separate compute chip through an interposer, essentially a standardized off-the-shelf product. "True" 3D IC, or memory-on-logic, uses hybrid bonding and through-silicon vias to attach DRAM directly onto the compute logic die itself, eliminating the interposer and shortening data paths. Reported gains run around 22% performance and 36% power, but it comes with a thermal mismatch between DRAM (tolerant to roughly 80°C) and logic (120-125°C), tricky bonding yields, and, crucially, a design that's specific to each customer rather than a standard catalog part.

## CXMT's 3D IC push is a workaround, not pure innovation
CXMT is blocked from the HBM market outright by US export controls. TSMC controls roughly 90% of global CoWoS packaging capacity and won't service leading Chinese AI firms, and HBM-specific manufacturing and packaging tools were added to export controls in December 2024. CXMT's 3D IC move reads more like "can't grow in HBM, so open a different niche instead." CXMT is reportedly already ahead of rivals in producing several 3D DRAM sample chips, though that "ahead" claim is specifically a comparison against Korea's Samsung and SK hynix, not a verified claim against the whole world including Micron or Winbond.

@@REF@@China's CXMT Is Betting On Customized DRAM To Circumvent U.S. Sanctions On HBM (wccftech, 2026-07-24)|https://wccftech.com/cxmt-custom-dram-us-sanctions-hbm/|https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/CXMT-3.jpg

## The real reason Samsung and SK hynix are cautious
Industry officials say custom, 3D-stacked DRAM is a fundamentally different business from the standardized, mass-produced DRAM that Samsung and SK hynix are built around, since every customer wants a different memory configuration and stacking method, making it hard to run profitably at scale.

But that's not the whole story. TrendForce reports Samsung is planning a 50% HBM capacity surge in 2026, and SK hynix is aiming to double its DRAM capacity in the second half of 2026 to catch up with Samsung. Both companies' capex and engineering headcount are already fully mobilized around expanding HBM4 and HBM4E. It's less that they're refusing 3D IC and more that they have no spare bandwidth for it right now. Samsung is in fact building a hybrid-bonding mass-production line at Pyeongtaek, but full-scale deployment isn't expected until 2029-2030, and SK hynix is separately hiring 3D-stacked DRAM design engineers in the US.

@@REF@@[News] Samsung Reportedly Builds Hybrid Bonding Mass Production Line; Full-Scale Deployment Seen in 2029-2030 (TrendForce, 2026-07-22)|https://www.trendforce.com/news/2026/07/22/news-samsung-reportedly-builds-hybrid-bonding-mass-production-line-full-scale-deployment-seen-in-2029-2030/|https://img.trendforce.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/22144509/BESI-hybrid-bonding-tool-20260722-624x407.jpg

Taiwan's Winbond also gets named alongside CXMT in this niche, but its core business has traditionally been specialty memory: low-power DRAM and NOR flash for automotive and industrial customers. Its role in 3D IC is a newer addition, tied to a recent TSMC deal to supply DRAM for wafer-on-wafer stacking.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is skipping the niche 3D IC market a missed opportunity for Samsung and SK hynix, or just the right call for now.

If Samsung's Pyeongtaek line comes online on schedule in 2029-2030, the caution will have been a matter of timing. If CXMT or Winbond lock in 3D IC customers before then, this caution will go down as a missed window instead.
kobeissi-margin-debt-net-credit-record:
A fresh sign of investors piling into stocks with borrowed money rather than cash has emerged. According to The Kobeissi Letter, net credit balances (the cash investors hold in brokerage accounts minus margin debt) fell $70 billion in June to a record negative $1.06 trillion. Margin debt itself climbed $895 billion over the same period to a record $1.50 trillion.

## Checking the numbers first
FINRA's own raw data confirms these figures almost exactly. June 2026 margin debt came to $1.502 trillion, and combined free credit balances across cash and margin accounts came to $440.9 billion. Subtract one from the other and you get negative $1.061 trillion, matching Kobeissi's figure closely.

@@REF@@This $1.5 Trillion Bomb Is Waiting to Blow Up Your Portfolio (Yahoo Finance/24/7 Wall St, 2026-07-25)|https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/1-5-trillion-bomb-waiting-131609949.html|https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/C6546FDF461C878C9BA01744731492C8CEA7B22A2941C3684FB9EB482F3D11CA/subgraphmysterio/resizefill_w1200_h624;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2F24_7_wall_st__718%2F87e712288d9edb5fbba769de6657ff28

## But 'broad risk appetite' may only be half the story
Kobeissi contrasts this with 2008, when investors held more cash and net credit balances were positive. Other sources, though, put both the 2000 dot-com peak (-$130 billion) and the 2008 peak (-$60 billion) in negative territory, suggesting this comparison may be mixing different measurement methodologies. That discrepancy isn't fully resolved as of this writing.

The stronger evidence is about where the leverage is actually concentrated. Per Crypto Briefing, leveraged ETFs hold about $179 billion in total assets, and 85% of that sits in just three sectors: tech, AI and semiconductors. On June 5, a 3x leveraged semiconductor ETF fell 31% in a single session. In July, South Korea's Kospi dropped 27% after SK hynix said it would slow AI memory expansion, triggering margin calls across roughly 1.2 million Korean brokerage accounts, about 10% of all trading accounts in the country, that had bet on the sector through leveraged ETFs.

@@REF@@Korea's AI Stock Rout Is Becoming a Lesson in Leveraged Excess (Bloomberg, 2026-07-14)|https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-14/korea-s-ai-stock-rout-is-becoming-a-lesson-in-leveraged-excess

@@CMP@@Kobeissi's read|Investor risk appetite is at unprecedented levels.|What other sources suggest|The leverage isn't spread broadly, it's concentrated in AI and semiconductor leveraged ETFs and derivatives, and that structure has already blown up once, in Korea.
"Investors love risk across the board" and "leverage is stacked in one AI-shaped corner of the market" paint very different pictures of what happens in the next pullback.

## Has margin debt historically warned of corrections
Three prior episodes of margin debt surging more than 65%, March 2000 (dot-com), July 2007 (financial crisis) and October 2021 (2022 bear market), all preceded market tops by roughly two to six months. This is being counted as a fourth instance of the pattern. The sample size is only three or four cycles, though, and some analysts note debt and markets tend to rise together, making this more of a coincident indicator than a precise timing tool.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is a record-low net credit balance a warning for the whole market, or a risk concentrated in one AI/semiconductor-shaped corner of it.

If cracks show up first in sector-specific leveraged products, as they did in Korea, it's the latter. If a pullback spreads across the broader market, the former reading was right. Margin debt doesn't cause a decline, but once one starts, it can make it bigger.
jukan-korea-memory-mega-mou-950b:
SK hynix agreed to supply $750 billion (about 1,085 trillion won) worth of advanced memory chips to Nvidia and other US tech giants over the next five years. The same day, Samsung Electronics signed a separate memorandum of understanding with Broadcom covering $200 billion (about 290 trillion won) in memory supply and foundry cooperation, also over five years. Both were announced by Kim Yong-beom, South Korea's presidential chief of staff for policy, during President Lee Jae-myung's Silicon Valley trip, relayed by chip-industry commentator Jukan on X.

## Samsung's $200 billion with Broadcom checks out
Samsung's own newsroom release confirms this almost word for word: "more than $200 billion across memory and foundry" over five years. Fortune independently confirmed the same figure through its own reporting.

@@REF@@Samsung Electronics and Broadcom Expand Strategic Collaboration Across Memory and Foundry Technologies (Samsung Newsroom, 2026-07-25)|https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-and-broadcom-expand-strategic-collaboration-across-memory-and-foundry-technologies|https://img.global.news.samsung.com/global/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/25142854/Samsung-Semiconductors-Memory-and-Foundry-Technologies-Broadcom-MoU_Thumb932_F.jpg

## But SK hynix's $750 billion doesn't match Jensen Huang's own number
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said, the same day, in his own words: "SK Group and I are announcing today that our two companies will enter into business partnerships that will represent over $500 billion of business together." That $500 billion spans not just SK hynix's memory supply but SK Telecom's AI infrastructure, an investment in Naver, Hyundai robotics, LG, and an AI Frontier Lab, the whole SK Group conglomerate. The government's $750 billion figure appears to layer on additional pieces, including a separate SK hynix-Microsoft supply deal, under the broader "SK-Nvidia and others" framing. The two numbers are counting different things, so reading $750 billion as "the memory contract with Nvidia alone" overstates what's actually there.

@@REF@@Nvidia, SK to announce $500 billion partnership, Jensen Huang says (Korea Herald, 2026-07-25)|https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10819890|https://wimg.heraldcorp.com/news/cms/2026/07/25/news-p.v1.20260725.84bb149612514e73b1311fe2aa1af0c0_T1.jpg

## Even 'MOU or not' is contested
SK hynix's own newsroom release calls this a "Letter of Intent," meaning a framework requiring further negotiation, not a binding contract. But policy chief Kim Yong-beom pushed back directly on that framing in a Seoul Economic Daily interview, saying "this isn't simply a corporate MOU, expect quite large, meaningful numbers from investment attraction, strategic alliances, and long-term contracts." The people announcing the deal and the people drafting it are describing it differently.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg/960px-DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg|A DRAM stick meant for a server slot. The core product in this deal is HBM4, bound for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform.|Smial · FAL 1.3|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DDR5_SDRAM_(with_scale)_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg

The products involved are reasonably specific. The SK hynix-Nvidia side names HBM4 for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; the Samsung-Broadcom side involves 2-nanometer-class foundry work and HBM4E. Around the same time, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei separately said the company had signed its own supply agreements with both Samsung and SK hynix, though no amount, product or duration was disclosed.

## So what's the thing to actually watch

serenity-googl-waymo-uber-split:

## What does the split actually mean
Reuters, Bloomberg and CNBC, all citing the FT report, describe something more specific: Waymo has told Uber it will launch its own independent app in exactly two cities, Austin and Atlanta, starting January 2028, ending exclusivity there.
That's not a company-wide breakup, it's an exclusivity deal ending in two markets. Under the existing contract, Waymo stays on Uber's platform in those cities through roughly May 2028. The two companies already ended their pilot in Phoenix in late June.
Cited friction points include Waymo's complaints about vehicle cleanliness and routing, Uber's complaints about vehicle unavailability in bad weather, and terms both sides called unsustainable. Waymo still runs its own app independently in 11 metro areas with over 500,000 weekly paid rides, and continues working with Uber elsewhere.

@@REF@@Uber and Waymo to end exclusivity arrangement in Atlanta and Austin (CNBC, 2026-07-24)|https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/24/uber-and-waymo-to-end-exclusivity-arrangement-in-atlanta-and-austin.html|https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/108255725-1769094685480-7VYxj_8U.jpg?v=1769094774&w=1920&h=1080

Serenity argues Uber should have chosen a neutral operator like Avride instead. But Uber already committed up to $375 million to Avride alongside Nebius back in October 2025.

kobeissi-datacenter-power-2035:
US data center electricity demand will surge 253% from 2026 levels to 194 gigawatts by 2035, equal to roughly 194 nuclear reactors' worth of power, with data centers' share of total US electricity use rising from about 6% today to 12% by 2030 and 20% by 2035, Kobeissi reports.

## Where does this number come from
The original source is BloombergNEF (BNEF), reported by Bloomberg on July 21. The 194 GW and 20% by 2035 figures match exactly.
But that forecast is itself 83% above BNEF's own previous estimate from December 2025 (106 GW), which was itself a big jump from BNEF's April 2025 estimate of 78 GW. That's three different BNEF numbers in 15 months: 78, then 106, then 194 gigawatts.
No secondary source reports the exact 253% figure verbatim. Tom's Hardware and DataCenterDynamics describe it as 83% above the prior forecast, while TechCrunch calls it four times today's level. Back-calculating from a roughly 55 GW 2026 baseline does get you to 194 divided by 55, or plus 253%, so the arithmetic checks out, but no secondary report states that baseline explicitly.

@@REF@@AI Boom to Drive Data Center Electricity Demand to 20% of US Total by 2035 (Bloomberg, 2026-07-21)|https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-21/data-centers-on-track-to-suck-up-a-fifth-of-us-power-use-by-2035

## What do other research houses say
EPRI puts the 2030 data center share at 9-17%. A World Resources Institute roundup of multiple forecasters shows a range from Lawrence Berkeley National Lab's 6.7-12% up to Boston Consulting Group's roughly 25%.
BNEF's 12% (2030) and 20% (2035) sit toward the upper-middle of that wide range. This is one estimate among several, not a settled consensus.

@@REF@@US data center power demand surpasses 150 GW, with PJM and ERCOT accounting for 60% of the facilities (Enerdatics, 2025-08-04)|https://www.enerdatics.com/insights/us-data-center-power-demand-surpasses-150-gw-with-pjm-and-ercot-accounting-for-60-of-the-facilities|https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/679098606c9b257593953e8d/6890dec13a94c8adb86d430c_PR%201.png

## Is the PJM concentration real
Yes. Of over 150 GW of announced US data center capacity tracked by Enerdatics, PJM holds roughly 45% (67 GW) and ERCOT in Texas about 13% (20 GW). BNEF projects PJM will send 34% of its electricity to data centers by 2035.
Per an Introl blog post from February 2026, PJM's queue for large new interconnections holds over 60 GW pending, with average waits exceeding four years. The national average interconnection wait has grown from under two years in 2008 to about five years now.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The bigger picture, power replacing chips as the AI buildout's real bottleneck, is already showing up in utility earnings (Southern Company's data-center-driven demand up 42%, Duke Energy with 7.6 GW under contract).
But the precise 2035 number should be read as the latest, most aggressive version of a forecast that's more than doubled in 15 months, not a fixed target.
trump-eu-301-investigation-bigtech-fines:
President Trump announced a Section 301 investigation into what he calls the EU robbing American companies through antitrust fines, citing $15 billion against Apple, $3 billion against Meta, $2.5 billion against Amazon, and a new $1 billion against Google, for a claimed cumulative total above $18 billion, and threatened a substantial tariff in response.

## Starting with Apple's $15 billion
The actual EU antitrust and Digital Markets Act fine against Apple in 2025-2026 was 500 million euros, about $571 million, issued in April 2025 over App Store anti-steering restrictions.
The $15 billion figure is actually the 2016 EU ruling ordering Ireland to recover roughly 13.1 billion euros plus interest in back taxes from Apple. That ruling was upheld by the EU's top court in September 2024, and Ireland withdrew about 14.25 billion euros, roughly $15.5 billion, from escrow in 2025. It's a tax case from 2016, not an antitrust fine, and 9to5Mac fact-checked this exact conflation in Trump's own post.

@@REF@@Trump vows retaliation over EU fines against Apple and other great US tech giants (9to5Mac, 2026-07-24)|https://9to5mac.com/2026/07/24/trump-vows-retaliation-over-eu-fines-against-apple-and-other-great-us-tech-giants/|https://i0.wp.com/9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2025/04/tim-cook-trump.jpg?resize=1200%2C628&quality=82&strip=all&ssl=1

## What about Meta and Amazon
Meta's actual DMA fine was 200 million euros, about $220 million, issued in April 2025 over its pay or consent ad model. No fine matching $3 billion was found, roughly a 15x overstatement.
No matching EU antitrust or DMA fine against Amazon was found at all. Amazon's actual live EU regulatory issue is a preliminary gatekeeper designation for AWS cloud services from June 2026, not a fine.

@@REF@@EU fines Meta and Apple under Digital Markets Act (NPR, 2025-04-23)|https://www.npr.org/2025/04/23/nx-s1-5373560/apple-meta-eu-tech-fines

## Did Google really just get fined $1 billion
That part checks out. The EU fined Google 890 million euros, about $1 billion, on July 23 over Search and Play Store DMA breaches. But cumulative above $18 billion doesn't hold up precisely.
Confirmed prior Google EU fines add up to roughly $13-15 billion: the 2017 Shopping case (2.42B euros), 2018 Android case (4.1-4.34B euros, upheld on appeal July 2, 2026), 2019 AdSense case (1.49B euros), and a September 2025 adtech fine (roughly $3.45B). That doesn't clearly clear $18 billion.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
Section 301 really is the same legal tool Trump used to launch tariffs against China. But he's also threatened the EU with 50% and 100% tariffs before without following through.
Three of the four dollar figures behind this threat don't check out or are inflated, and only Google's new fine is accurate. Whether that shaky foundation still ends in real tariffs, or another walked-back threat, is a separate question worth watching regardless.
jensen-open-models-letter:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang posted on X for the first time on July 24, using it to share a letter titled Open Weights and American AI Leadership, arguing open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity and protect national AI sovereignty.

## Who actually signed
Per Fortune and Tom's Hardware, the letter launched with roughly 25 signers, Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, Palantir, Hugging Face, IBM, Mistral, Dell, and a16z among them. OpenAI and Google weren't on it.
Forbes reported the signer list roughly doubled to about 50 within a day, as OpenAI, Google, AMD, Cisco and GitHub joined late. Anthropic and Amazon never signed at all.

@@REF@@Jensen Huang just used his first ever X post to warn the AI industry not to make the mistake that software narrowly avoided in the 1980s (Fortune, 2026-07-24)|https://fortune.com/2026/07/24/jensen-huang-open-source-letter-nvidia-kimi/|https://fortune.com/img-assets/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/GettyImages-2286326398-e1784913912763.jpg?resize=1200,600

## Why did Anthropic sit this out
Per Axios, July 27, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei declined to join, citing a safety concern that open-weight models cannot be recalled once released.
That's a substantive safety objection, not just competitive positioning. The timing is notable too. Four days earlier, reports surfaced that the White House was reviving a push to restrict Chinese open-weight models, including Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, released July 16, accused of distilling US models, and days after Xi Jinping made his own openness pitch at China's World AI Conference on July 17, announcing a rival body, the World AI Cooperation Organization, with 29 countries signed on.

@@REF@@Big Tech lines up in support of open-weight AI (Axios, 2026-07-27)|https://www.axios.com/2026/07/27/nvidia-anthropic-openai-open-weight-debate|https://images.axios.com/T0kiLOXo8ikXMd6Vj1NWbBlEfHQ=/0x0:1920x1080/1366x768/2026/03/26/1774548278869.jpeg

## Why is Nvidia the one pushing this
Per Yahoo Finance, Nvidia controls roughly 81% of the data-center AI chip market, and more open models spreads chip demand across many more buyers instead of concentrating it in a few efficiency-optimizing closed API providers, a commercial interest baked into the position.
Huang himself is quoted saying more AI use means you'll have to sell more Nvidia computers. Forbes summed it up as every signatory argues for openness in someone else's yard. Nvidia itself owns proprietary CUDA and is a $26 billion investor in OpenAI.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
Whether to read this letter as industry-wide consensus or a coalition that joined at different times for different self-interested reasons comes down to who signed when, and who didn't.
What actually matters is whether this shapes Washington's real export and procurement rules, and how the signatories answer the cannot be recalled safety concern Anthropic raised by staying out.

kobeissi-oracle-cds-record: Oracle's cost of insuring against a default has hit a record, with five-year credit default swaps trading near 203 basis points, meaning investors now pay roughly $203,000 a year to insure $10 million of the company's debt against non-payment, The Kobeissi Letter reports. S&P Global Ratings downgraded Oracle to BBB-, one notch above junk, on July 9th, citing the company's fast-growing spending on AI data centers.
